claims.text: Rapid high-temperature shock synthesis traps a homogeneous, metastable solid solution in Fe-Ni-Cr-Co-Cu high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles.
The kinetically trapped solid solution delays surface premelting relative to particles produced by slower thermal methods.
The kinetically trapped solid solution elevates the onset temperature of melting relative to particles produced by slower thermal methods.
Rapid shock synthesis limits the time available for atomic diffusion.
Limiting atomic diffusion during synthesis suppresses elemental segregation and produces a uniform chemical state.
The homogeneous solid-solution structure resists early elemental segregation at the nanoparticle surface.
Delayed surface segregation postpones the melting transition and raises its onset temperature.
Shock-synthesized particles will show a sharper and more abrupt melting transition than slower-synthesized particles.
Shock-synthesized particles will show fewer signs of surface premelting than slower-synthesized particles.
Slow thermal processing permits partial equilibration of Fe-Ni-Cr-Co-Cu high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles.
Slow thermal processing produces earlier surface elemental segregation than rapid shock synthesis.
Earlier surface segregation in the slower-synthesized baseline results in a lower melting-onset temperature.
Earlier surface segregation in the slower-synthesized baseline results in more gradual premelting behavior.
Nanoparticle size effects and minor compositional fluctuations may affect the magnitude of the melting-onset shift and the kinetics of melting.
